evidence_sources.title: Probabilistic principal component analysis
evidence_sources.version: Columbia-hosted copy of the final Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B 61(3):611-622 (1999) article. All 12 PDF pages visually read; printed page equals PDF page plus 610. Later online-publication metadata are not the article year.

claims.statement: For latent dimension q<d, let x~Normal(0,I_q) and t=Wx+mu+epsilon with independent epsilon~Normal(0,sigma^2 I_d), sigma^2>0. Then t~Normal(mu,C), C=WW^T+sigma^2 I_d. The observed-data model is a normalized full-rank Gaussian; the low-rank loading contribution does not make the positive-noise density singular. Isotropic noise is a stronger restriction than the arbitrary diagonal noise of factor analysis.

evidence.locator: Sections 2.1 and 3.1, Equations 1-5, printed pp. 612 and 614 / PDF pp. 2 and 4

claims.statement: For sample covariance S=N^(-1)sum_n(t_n-mu)(t_n-mu)^T at the sample-mean mu, take its q leading eigenpairs U_q,Lambda_q. The likelihood solution has sigma^2 equal to the mean of the d-q discarded eigenvalues and W=U_q(Lambda_q-sigma^2 I)^(1/2)R for any orthogonal R. Rank(S)>q ensures positive residual variance. Tied eigenvalues can make loading columns vanish: for spectrum (2,1,1) and q=2, sigma^2=1 and the effective loading rank is one. Neither the columns nor latent coordinates are uniquely identified.

evidence.locator: Sections 3.2-3.3, Equations 7-8, printed pp. 614-615 / PDF pp. 4-5; Appendix A, Equations 10-21 and equal-eigenvalue example, pp. 618-621 / PDF pp. 8-11

claims.statement: With M=W^T W+sigma^2 I, the latent posterior is Normal(M^(-1)W^T(t-mu),sigma^2 M^(-1)). Mapping its mean back through W generally shrinks the observation within the loading subspace; it is not the ordinary orthogonal PCA reconstruction. When W has full column rank, W(W^T W)^(-1)M times the posterior mean, plus mu, recovers the orthogonal projection. The zero-noise limit loses a nonsingular ambient density for q<d.

evidence.locator: Equations 6 and 9 and Section 3.4, printed pp. 614-615 / PDF pp. 4-5; curator finite shrinkage and rank qualification

claims.statement: The E-step computes posterior first and second latent moments using the old W and noise variance. The M-step fits W by observation-latent cross-moments times the inverse summed latent second moment, then updates noise from the expected squared residual using the new W and old posterior moments. Exact well-defined EM makes likelihood nondecreasing, but a zero-loading initialization can remain stationary at an inferior isotropic solution. The existence of a principal-eigenspace maximum does not guarantee successful convergence from every initialization.

evidence.locator: Appendix B, Equations 25-31, printed pp. 621-622 / PDF pp. 11-12; Appendix A stationary-point analysis, pp. 619-620 / PDF pp. 9-10; curator zero-loading example

limitations: Latent dimension is a model choice. When residual eigenvalues all vanish, the formal noise estimate reaches the zero-variance boundary, outside the nonsingular positive-noise model. Latent rotations and covariance eigenvalue ties prevent unique axes without additional conventions.
The conditional mean is a probabilistic latent summary, not automatic recovery of physical factors or minimum input-space reconstruction error. Isotropic Gaussian noise can be misspecified.

Missing-at-random integration and mixtures of PPCA are extensions described in the paper; they are not properties of an arbitrary imputation scheme or aliases for this single Gaussian model. This record does not cover supervised PCA.

All 12 primary pages were read. Finite arithmetic checks one exact EM step, posterior shrinkage, rotation/rank ambiguity and a stationary initialization. The Tobamovirus illustrations and author software were not reproduced.

aio_mappings.rationale: PPCA is a specific mathematical probability model within the pinned Model class.

Its likelihood eigensolution spans a principal subspace, but the normalized latent model, posterior uncertainty and shrinkage differ from the task-scoped PCA record. This relation preserves the model/task distinction.

evidence_sources.title: Principal Curves
evidence_sources.version: Author-hosted JSTOR scan of Journal of the American Statistical Association 84(406):502-516 (June 1989), reached through the Stanford URL redirecting to hastie.su.domains. All 16 PDF pages visually read. Page 1 is a download cover; pages 2-16 correspond to printed pages 502-516. The cover access date is not the publication date.

claims.statement: For a distribution with density and finite second moments, the original definition uses a smooth unit-speed non-self-intersecting curve f over a closed interval, possibly unbounded, with finite length inside each finite ball. The projection index lambda_f(x) selects the largest parameter among nearest points. Self-consistency requires E[X|lambda_f(X)=lambda]=f(lambda) almost everywhere. Closed curves such as circles require the extension discussed by the authors; they do not literally satisfy the original interval/injectivity definition.

evidence.locator: Section 2, Equation 3 and Definition 1, printed pp. 504-505 / PDF pp. 4-5; Appendix opening, p. 514 / PDF p. 14

claims.statement: The original sample estimator alternates closest-point projection onto a polygonal curve with coordinatewise smoothing against the resulting arc-length indices. It usually starts from the first principal-component line. Locally weighted running-line smoothing with a neighborhood span approximates the population conditional mean; smoothing splines are an alternative. The paper does not prove convergence or per-step decrease of the sample distance criterion, and population conditional-mean updates can have endpoint discontinuities.

evidence.locator: Sections 4-5.3, printed pp. 506-507 / PDF pp. 6-7; Section 5.5, p. 509 / PDF p. 9

claims.statement: Under the paper’s regularity and bounded smooth perturbation class, self-consistency is equivalent to stationarity of expected squared nearest-curve distance, not global optimality. A self-consistent straight line is a covariance principal-component line; the converse need not hold for arbitrary distributions. Ellipsoidal distributions can have multiple self-consistent eigenvector lines with different reconstruction risks. Thus the definition alone does not select a unique leading curve or guarantee minimum reconstruction error.

evidence.locator: Section 3, Propositions 1-4, printed pp. 505-506 / PDF pp. 5-6; Appendix proof, pp. 514-516 / PDF pp. 14-16; curator analytic Gaussian-line and nonlinear conditional-mean examples

claims.statement: A noisy generating curve need not be self-consistent for the distribution it generates. In the paper’s circular Gaussian-noise example, the population principal-circle radius is displaced outward, while averaging over a finite arc contracts the local mean. These model and smoothing biases are distinct and need not cancel. Repeated coordinatewise cross-validation inside the fitting loop can select progressively smaller spans and nearly interpolate the data.

evidence.locator: Sections 5.4-6, Figure 7 and Equation 8, printed pp. 508-510 / PDF pp. 8-10

limitations: The paper does not establish existence or uniqueness of principal curves for every density. Its thin-tube construction supplies distributions for a specified compact curve, not a general existence theorem.

Smoothing strength, initialization, curve endpoints and periodic versus nonperiodic treatment affect estimates. Regularized spline objectives and higher-dimensional principal surfaces require additional assumptions; their existence or global convergence is not established here.
A curve summary need not identify a causal latent path or generate a normalized probability density. Nearest-point projection is not the latent posterior of PPCA or GTM.

All 16 PDF pages, including the cover, appendix and references, were read. Analytic moment calculations check scope boundaries; collider alignment, gold-assay bootstrap results and author implementations were not reproduced.

aio_mappings.rationale: Principal curves provide a one-dimensional geometric summary of multivariate observations, including noisy observations away from the curve. The pinned target is a dimensionality-reduction task; this mapping does not assert task/mathematical-method equivalence or exact manifold recovery.

evidence_sources.title: A Simplified Neuron Model as a Principal Component Analyzer
evidence_sources.version: Author-hosted scan of Journal of Mathematical Biology 15:267-273 (1982). All seven PDF pages visually read; printed page equals PDF page plus 266. The title and journal metadata are visible on the first page.

claims.statement: For current input x, weights w, scalar output y=w^T x and positive gain eta, the truncated rule is w_new=w+eta*y*(x-y*w). Each synaptic increment uses its input, its weight and the common scalar output. The negative eta*y^2*w term regulates Hebbian growth. This drops second- and higher-order gain terms from explicit normalization of w+eta*y*x, and therefore does not preserve unit norm exactly at a finite step.

evidence.locator: Equations 1-6, printed pp. 267-269 / PDF pp. 1-3; Section 4, Equations 11-15, pp. 271-272 / PDF pp. 5-6; curator finite-norm example

claims.statement: When the current input is independent of current weights, averaging the truncated increment per unit gain gives Cw-(w^T Cw)w, where C=E[xx^T]. The associated mean differential equation has signed top unit eigenvectors as attracting equilibria when C has a positive simple largest eigenvalue and initialization has a nonzero component along its eigenvector. In eigenvector coordinates, ratios to the leading coordinate decay according to the eigenvalue gap. This is a mean-ODE result with explicit conditions.

evidence.locator: Section 3, Equations 7-8 and theorem, printed pp. 269-270 / PDF pp. 3-4; curator positive-eigenvalue qualification

claims.statement: For zero-mean inputs, C is the covariance, and the leading learned response corresponds to the largest-variance principal component. Without centering, C includes the outer product of the mean and the rule targets maximum quadratic mean instead. Mean subtraction is not part of the displayed update. The paper analyzes a single neuron and does not derive a full multi-component PCA network or independent-component separator.

evidence.locator: Section 3, printed p. 270 / PDF p. 4; Section 5, p. 272 / PDF p. 6

claims.statement: The source invokes stochastic-approximation results with suitable input regularity and a decreasing gain, such as a gain proportional to inverse time; it does not spell out a complete general stochastic convergence theorem. A small fixed gain is discussed as an approximation to mean dynamics, not a guarantee of exact almost-sure convergence. Zero or mean-ODE orthogonal starts and repeated leading eigenvalues require separate treatment. Large discrete gains can increase weight magnitude instead of controlling it.

evidence.locator: Section 3, printed pp. 269-270 / PDF pp. 3-4; curator stationary-direction, finite-norm and large-gain examples

limitations: The PCA interpretation requires centered finite-second-moment inputs and the relevant stationary/input assumptions. Correlation across time, changing distributions and dependence between current input and weights need a justified analysis.
The first-order discrete rule is not exact normalization. Step size and initialization matter; the mean-ODE theorem does not establish global stability of every finite-gain implementation.
With a repeated largest eigenvalue there is no unique principal direction, and sign is intrinsically ambiguous. A single unit yields one direction rather than an ordered orthogonal basis.
All seven source pages were read. Finite arithmetic and analytic mean-flow checks were performed; no neuron training, historical simulation or biological experiment was reproduced.

aio_mappings.rationale: For centered inputs and the stated conditions, this learning rule estimates one leading PCA direction. The pinned target is task-scoped PCA, not this synaptic update or a complete multi-component algorithm.
The update uses observations without supervised targets. This is an algorithm related to the pinned learning task, not a forced subclass of its preprocessing-defined TrainingStrategy parent.

ppca.pagination: PDF page p corresponds to printed page p+610 (611–622).
notes: Pages 1–3: PCA variance and orthogonal reconstruction objectives; latent Gaussian factor analysis with diagonal noise; historical Lawley/Anderson–Rubin scaled eigenvector solutions precede this presentation. PPCA is not claimed to be the first probabilistic latent-factor idea.

Pages 4–5, equations 2–9: latent x~N(0,I), isotropic conditional noise sigma^2 I, t marginal N(mu, WW^T+sigma^2 I). The MLE mean is the sample mean and S uses denominator N. W_ML=U_q(Lambda_q-sigma^2 I)^(1/2)R; sigma^2 is the mean discarded sample eigenvalue. R is an arbitrary orthogonal latent rotation. Posterior mean M^-1 W^T(t-mu), covariance sigma^2 M^-1, M=W^T W+sigma^2 I.

Page 5: posterior-mean reconstruction is shrunk and generally not the ordinary orthogonal least-squares projection. A full-column-rank correction recovers that projection. As sigma tends to zero the ambient density becomes singular when q<d; this is a valid degenerate distribution but no nonsingular d-dimensional Gaussian density. Isotropic noise yields rotation covariance, distinct from unrestricted diagonal-noise factor analysis.

Pages 6–8: missing-at-random values may be integrated in EM; the 38-example, 18-dimensional Tobamovirus illustration randomly removes values with probability 0.2 (136 missing values). A three-component PPCA mixture is a separate extension, not the single Gaussian model. The covariance degree-of-freedom count dq+1-q(q-1)/2 presumes the ordinary generic-rank situation and excludes the mean. Table 1 bootstrap prediction errors are historical dataset-specific illustrations, not reproduced outcomes or universal superiority.

Pages 9–11, Appendix A equations 10–21: stationary loading columns correspond to covariance eigenvectors or zero loading. Positive residual variance at the solution follows from rank(S)>q. Nonprincipal solutions are saddles under the stated nondegenerate conditions; rotational and equal-eigenvalue ambiguity remains. With spectrum (2,1,1), q=2, sigma^2=1, the second loading vanishes and effective rank is one. Thus q columns need not have rank q. A blanket guaranteed convergence from all initializations is unsupported; W=0 is stationary and can remain fixed under EM.

Pages 11–12, Appendix B equations 25–31: E[x] and E[xx^T] use old parameters; update W using cross-moments and second moments; update sigma using the new W and the old posterior moments. In compact equation 30 the first W is old and the second W-tilde is new, explicitly clarified on p.622. Data can enter through covariance products without explicitly materializing the d by d matrix; the stated computational comparison assumes q much smaller than d and depends on iteration count. Nonorthogonal loading columns can span the principal subspace; latent rotations are unidentifiable.

Page 12 references read: Bishop–Tipping 1998 hierarchical latent-variable visualization, Dony–Haykin 1995 optimal adaptive transform coding, Rubin–Thayer 1982 factor-analysis EM, and older latent-factor/PCA sources offer distinct provisional follow-up identities. No implementation or historical experiment reproduced.

curves.pagination: PDF page 1 is a JSTOR cover; PDF pages 2–16 correspond to printed pages 502–516 (p+500).
notes: Pages 2–4: principal curves summarize a multivariate distribution symmetrically without a designated response variable. The formal population definition uses a smooth unit-speed non-self-intersecting curve over a closed possibly unbounded interval, finite length in every finite ball, a density and finite second moments. The closest-point projection index breaks ties by taking the largest minimizing parameter. Self-consistency means f(lambda)=E[X|lambda_f(X)=lambda] almost everywhere. It is a population conditional-expectation property, not merely any nonlinear embedding or smooth curve fit.

Pages 5–6, propositions 1–4: a self-consistent straight line passes through the mean and is a covariance eigenvector line. The converse is not true for general distributions; ellipsoidal distributions provide self-consistent principal-component lines. Under the stated regularity, principal curves are stationary points of expected squared projection distance with respect to bounded smooth perturbations, not necessarily local or global minima. The population alternating conditional-mean and projection operations reduce distance when well defined, but the mean curve can fail differentiability or have endpoint discontinuities; convergence of the curves is not proved.

Pages 6–9, sections 5.1–5.5: finite data are represented by a polygon ordered by arc length. Each observation is projected onto the closest segment; coordinatewise scatterplot smoothing over those indices approximates the conditional mean. Exact empirical conditional means usually interpolate singleton observations, so smoothing matters. The paper uses locally weighted running-line fits with a nearest-neighbor span and tricube weights; splines are an alternative. It explicitly cannot prove practical-algorithm convergence or per-step decrease of its sample criterion. Fixed decreasing spans are a heuristic; repeated coordinatewise cross-validation can shrink spans until nearly interpolating the data.

Page 9: spline penalty sum_i||x_i-f(lambda_i)||^2 + mu integral_0^1||f double-prime||^2 differs from the pure population definition. The fixed parameter interval prevents arbitrary interval stretching from evading curvature penalties. This is a regularized variant; the authors claim neither existence of its minimizer nor global convergence.

Pages 5,9–10: spherical distributions admit self-consistent lines and, in a closed-curve extension, a circle with radius E||X||. The paper explicitly notes a circle lies outside the interval/injectivity definition and discusses periodic smoothers. Thus the core object need not be unique or recover a generating curve. Model bias for noisy curved latent paths differs from the flattening bias introduced by smoothing. In the Gaussian-noisy circle example r*=E sqrt((rho+e1)^2+e2^2)>rho; a neighborhood average multiplies r* by sin(theta/2)/(theta/2). Cancellation is not a general unbiasedness result.

Pages 10–13: historical applications are collider-magnet alignment and 250 paired log gold assays. The collider implementation fits deviations from a known theoretical path and uses application-specific curvature, endpoint, fixed-magnet and resistant-fitting modifications; its percent-moved statistic is not a general algorithm guarantee. The assay example uses an errors-in-variables variant, equal error variances and residual bootstrap with a sqrt(2) correction. These are scoped illustrations, not newly reproduced experiments.

Pages 13–14: principal surfaces extend the idea to two-dimensional parameters; this paper says rigorous justification is incomplete and points to Hastie 1984. Carroll polynomial factor analysis, Etezadi-Amoli–McDonald nonlinear factor analysis, and Shepard–Carroll parametric nonlinear-structure representations are distinct prior methods, not aliases.

Pages 14–16 appendix: proves closest-point index existence, measure-zero ambiguous projections under regularity, and the stationary-distance equivalence through dominated convergence; describes densities in a thin normal tube around a compact curve that have the prescribed curve as principal. This is not an existence proof for every arbitrary density. Closed curves require a slight modification explicitly noted in the appendix. All appendix and reference pages were visually read.

oja.pagination: PDF page p corresponds to printed page p+266 (267–273).
notes: Pages 1–2, equations 1–3: a scalar linear neuron output y=w^T x and an explicitly Euclidean-normalized Hebbian update motivate a first-order small-gain expansion. Dropping terms of order gain squared yields w_new=w+gain*y*(x-y*w), now known as Oja learning. The output-dependent negative term regulates Hebbian growth. Exact normalized Hebbian learning and its truncated update are distinct; the latter does not preserve norm exactly at a finite step.

Pages 3–4, equations 4–8: with current input independent of current weights, averaging uses C=E[xx^T]. The associated differential equation is dz/dt=Cz-(z^T C z)z. The paper discusses diminishing gain and regularity assumptions through stochastic-approximation references without fully proving those hypotheses. It does not establish arbitrary fixed-gain discrete convergence or unconditional stability.

Page 4 theorem: for a positive semidefinite C with a simple largest eigenvalue, the mean ODE converges to the signed top unit eigenvector when the initial projection onto it is nonzero. The positive leading-eigenvalue, nonzero-projection and eigengap conditions should remain explicit. The coordinate ratio satisfies d(theta_i)/dt=(lambda_i-lambda_1)theta_i. Orthogonal or zero starts and repeated leading eigenvalues do not yield a unique signed leading direction under that statement.

Page 4: centered inputs make C the covariance and the scalar output a leading PCA component. Noncentered inputs instead maximize quadratic mean under a norm constraint; mean subtraction is not part of the rule. For a fixed signal plus isotropic noise, the leading direction is a matched-filter example under those assumptions. This is not empirical biological validation.

Pages 4–6, equations 9–15: the paper extends the expansion to differentiable homogeneous normalization functions and general increments. The Euclidean example gives the y-squared feedback term. Its phrase homogeneous for any scalar requires the usual positive scaling for a norm; no assertion of odd homogeneity of the Euclidean norm is imported. General norm constraints are background, not aliases of the specific Oja rule.

Pages 6–7: the analyzed model is one neuron; lateral interactions or multi-output networks are explicitly outside its analysis. Biological motivation and feature-detection references do not establish experimental neural implementation. References include Oja–Karhunen 1981 stochastic eigenvector approximation, Ljung 1977 recursive stochastic algorithms, and Kohonen 1982 self-organizing maps. All reference pages were read.

claims.statement: For M training points and a positive-semidefinite kernel k, form K_ij=k(x_i,x_j) and Kc=H K H with H=I-11^T/M. ./reviews/structured/20261012T005354Z-author-group-components/review.md:65:For fixed document length and author-position count, word tokens, author tokens and a discrete timestamp contribute shared matrix columns to a vector S. The positive-hidden joint contains exp(sum_i[-log(t_i)-log(t_i)^2/2+S_i*log(t_i)]). Changing variables to y=log(t), including the Jacobian, gives y conditional on all visible observations distributed as N(S,I), and visible mass proportional to exp(||S||^2/2). The positive-hidden mean is exp(S_i+1/2), not S_i; positive coordinates do not by themselves create a normalized simplex of topics. Missing visible modalities generally produce mixtures after marginalization rather than the same single Gaussian with their columns set to zero. The source fits approximate joint or conditional likelihood using contrastive divergence and Gaussian weight shrinkage. Conditional training clamps words and time while reconstructing authors. Replicated categorical author positions use occurrence counts as sufficient statistics, including when a reconstruction repeats an author. Equation 8 instead displays a presence indicator and prints A-1 as a word-sum limit; the general statistic requires author counts and the vocabulary dimension. The exact fixed-length likelihood gradient contrasts observed count-times-S statistics with their model expectation, with an additional prior gradient if regularized. Short-chain CD approximates that expectation and is not exact maximum likelihood. A common orthogonal transformation of the hidden rows of all interaction matrices preserves ||S||^2 and therefore every fixed-size visible probability. It also preserves an isotropic Gaussian weight penalty. Such shrinkage consequently does not remove all latent rotation ambiguity or guarantee a uniquely interpretable set or number of components. The source's suggestion that the prior addresses nonidentifiability or enables automatic component selection has this mathematical boundary. Limitations: Finite categorical sample spaces make the partition function finite for each fixed number of word and author positions and finite weights. The source does not specify a normalized distribution over unbounded document lengths. Independent author positions can repeat authors; this is not automatically a distribution over unique author sets. The evaluated timestamps are discrete years or months. Proposed Gaussian or Beta visible attributes require their own compatible joint and normalization analysis. Broad PCA comparisons do not establish equivalence to probabilistic PCA with Gaussian observations. The reported author/recipient evaluation retrieves training documents by cosine similarity in latent space and scores the first result sharing an author or recipient. This is not exact author-set conditional-probability ranking. Treatment of missing target-modality features in embeddings is underspecified; no data-leakage allegation or unprovided implementation is inferred. Selected NIPS and single-user email data, random splits, twenty components and best reported iteration scores provide bounded empirical evidence. Finite checks verify fixed-size probabilities, a gradient, rotation invariance and missing-modality mixtures, not historical software, convergence or the reported benchmark.
